claim: Avian influenza outbreaks have been occurring on smallholder poultry farms in Asia for two decades.
source: Avian influenza outbreaks have been occurring on smallholder poultry farms in Asia for two decades.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that draws on established knowledge about avian influenza in Asia.

claim: In small broiler flocks (≤16 birds/flock) the estimated probability of harvest was 56% higher when an outbreak occurred.
source: We found that in small broiler flocks (≤16 birds/flock) the estimated probability of harvest was 56% higher when an outbreak occurred, and 214% higher if an outbreak with sudden deaths occurred in the same month.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the longitudinal survey presented in the manuscript.

claim: In small broiler flocks (≤16 birds/flock) the estimated probability of harvest was 214% higher if an outbreak with sudden deaths occurred in the same month.
source: We found that in small broiler flocks (≤16 birds/flock) the estimated probability of harvest was 56% higher when an outbreak occurred, and 214% higher if an outbreak with sudden deaths occurred in the same month.
evidence: This claim is supported by data analysis from the longitudinal survey.

claim: Vaccination and disinfection were strongly and positively correlated with the number of birds.
source: Vaccination and disinfection were strongly and positively correlated with the number of birds.
evidence: This claim is supported by statistical analysis of the survey data.

claim: Small-scale farmers tend to rely on rapid sale of birds to mitigate losses from diseases.
source: Small-scale farmers – the overwhelming majority of poultry producers in low-income countries – tend to rely on rapid sale of birds to mitigate losses from diseases.
evidence: This claim is supported by the data analysis showing increased harvest rates during outbreaks.

claim: Reactive behavior of rapid sale has the potential to enhance onward transmission as depopulated birds are sent to markets or trading networks.
source: As depopulated birds are sent to markets or trading networks, this reactive behavior has the potential to enhance onward transmission.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observed behavior and knowledge of disease transmission pathways.

claim: Livestock production systems have been a major driver of novel pathogen emergence events over the past two decades.
source: Livestock production systems have been a major driver of novel pathogen emergence events over the past two decades (Gao et al., 2013; Guan et al., 2002; Rohr et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Human behavioral changes like hygiene improvements or social distancing affect the conditions enabling emergence and spread of new diseases in human populations.
source: The conditions enabling the emergence and spread of a new disease in the human population partly depend on human behavioral changes, like hygiene improvements or social distancing, in the face of epidemiological risks (Funk et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Farmers adapt their farm management to maximize animal production and welfare while limiting cost in a constantly changing ecological and economic environment.
source: The same observation applies to disease emergence and spread in livestock populations as farmers adapt their farm management to maximize animal production and welfare while limiting cost in a constantly changing ecological and economic environment (Chilonda and Van Huylenbroeck, 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Poultry farming is now the most important source of animal protein for the human population.
source: It is now the most important source of animal protein for the human population and the industry is changing rapidly (FAOSTAT, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to FAOSTAT data.

claim: The highly pathogenic form of avian influenza due to the H5N1 subtype initially emerged in China in 1996.
source: The link between poultry sector expansion and pathogen emergence is exemplified by the worldwide spread of the highly pathogenic form of avian influenza (AI) due to the H5N1 subtype of influenza A, after its initial emergence in China in 1996 (Guan et al., 2002; Guan and Smith, 2013).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) causes severe symptoms in the most vulnerable bird species including chicken, turkey, and quail.
source: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) causes severe symptoms in the most vulnerable bird species (including chicken, turkey, and quail), with mortality rates as high as 100% reported in broiler flocks (OIE, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to OIE documentation.

claim: Mortality rates as high as 100% have been reported in broiler flocks affected by HPAI.
source: Highly Pathogenic Avian Influenza (HPAI) causes severe symptoms in the most vulnerable bird species (including chicken, turkey, and quail), with mortality rates as high as 100% reported in broiler flocks (OIE, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to OIE documentation.

claim: Some subtypes of AI viruses including H5N1, H5N6, H7N9 and H9N2 have caused infection in humans.
source: Some subtypes of AI viruses have caused infection in humans, including H5N1, H5N6, H7N9 and H9N2, with potentially severe illness and, in the cases of H7N9 and H5N1, a high case-fatality rate (Chen et al., 2013; Claas et al., 1998; Peiris et al., 1999; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: H7N9 and H5N1 infections in humans have a high case-fatality rate.
source: Some subtypes of AI viruses have caused infection in humans, including H5N1, H5N6, H7N9 and H9N2, with potentially severe illness and, in the cases of H7N9 and H5N1, a high case-fatality rate (Chen et al., 2013; Claas et al., 1998; Peiris et al., 1999; Yang et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Reports of human-to-human transmission of H5N1, H5N6, H7N9 and H9N2 have been either absent or anecdotal.
source: So far, reports of human-to-human transmission of these subtypes of influenza have been either absent or anecdotal, but the risk that they make the leap to a human pandemic is a persistent if unquantifiable threat to public health (Imai et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and represents established knowledge.

claim: The risk that avian influenza subtypes make the leap to a human pandemic is a persistent if unquantifiable threat to public health.
source: So far, reports of human-to-human transmission of these subtypes of influenza have been either absent or anecdotal, but the risk that they make the leap to a human pandemic is a persistent if unquantifiable threat to public health (Imai et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation and involves speculation about future risk.

claim: HPAI does not persist in poultry populations in most affected countries.
source: While HPAI does not persist in poultry populations in most affected countries, it has become endemic in parts of Asia and Africa and is periodically re-introduced into other areas like Europe and North America (Lai et al., 2016; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: HPAI has become endemic in parts of Asia and Africa.
source: While HPAI does not persist in poultry populations in most affected countries, it has become endemic in parts of Asia and Africa and is periodically re-introduced into other areas like Europe and North America (Lai et al., 2016; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: HPAI is periodically re-introduced into areas like Europe and North America.
source: While HPAI does not persist in poultry populations in most affected countries, it has become endemic in parts of Asia and Africa and is periodically re-introduced into other areas like Europe and North America (Lai et al., 2016; Li et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Major factors influencing HPAI epidemiology in affected countries include farm disinfection, poultry vaccination, and marketing of potentially infected birds through trade networks.
source: In affected countries, major factors influencing HPAI epidemiology appear to be farm disinfection, poultry vaccination, and marketing of potentially infected birds through trade networks, all of which depend on farmers' management decisions (Biswas et al., 2009; Desvaux et al., 2011; Fasina et al., 2011; Henning et al., 2009; Kung et al., 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: An anthropological study in Cambodia showed that high levels of farmer risk awareness associated with HPAI did not translate into major changes in their farming practices.
source: An anthropological study in Cambodia showed that high levels of farmer risk awareness associated with HPAI did not translate into major changes in their farming practices (Hickler, 2007).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Qualitative investigations in Vietnam, Bangladesh, China, and Indonesia reported that farmers sometimes urgently sell or cull diseased poultry flocks as a way to mitigate economic losses.
source: Qualitative investigations conducted in Vietnam, Bangladesh, China, and Indonesia reported that farmers sometimes urgently sell or cull diseased poultry flocks as a way to mitigate economic losses, but evidence of this behavior's onward epidemiological impact was not available (Biswas et al., 2009; Delabouglise et al., 2016; Padmawati and Nichter, 2008; Sultana et al., 2012; Zhang and Pan, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Evidence of the onward epidemiological impact of urgent sale or culling of diseased poultry flocks was not available from qualitative investigations in Vietnam, Bangladesh, China, and Indonesia.
source: Qualitative investigations conducted in Vietnam, Bangladesh, China, and Indonesia reported that farmers sometimes urgently sell or cull diseased poultry flocks as a way to mitigate economic losses, but evidence of this behavior's onward epidemiological impact was not available (Biswas et al., 2009; Delabouglise et al., 2016; Padmawati and Nichter, 2008; Sultana et al., 2012; Zhang and Pan, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to published literature.

claim: Changes in farm management caused by variations in epidemiological risk have not been quantified for any livestock system, primarily because of the lack of combined epidemiological and behavioural data in longitudinal studies of livestock disease.
source: Changes in farm management caused by variations in epidemiological risk have not been quantified for any livestock system that we are aware of, primarily because of the lack of combined epidemiological and behavioural data in longitudinal studies of livestock disease (Hidano et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Ifft et al., 2011 compared the evolution of chicken farm sizes and disease prevention in administrative areas with different levels of HPAI prevalence in Vietnam.
source: Ifft et al., 2011 compared the evolution of chicken farm sizes and disease prevention in administrative areas with different levels of HPAI prevalence in Vietnam, and Hidano and Gates, 2019 modelled the effect of cattle mortality and production performance on the frequency of sales and culling in New Zealand dairy farms.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Hidano and Gates, 2019 modelled the effect of cattle mortality and production performance on the frequency of sales and culling in New Zealand dairy farms.
source: Ifft et al., 2011 compared the evolution of chicken farm sizes and disease prevention in administrative areas with different levels of HPAI prevalence in Vietnam, and Hidano and Gates, 2019 modelled the effect of cattle mortality and production performance on the frequency of sales and culling in New Zealand dairy farms.
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Studies by Ifft et al., 2011 and Hidano and Gates, 2019 observed dynamics over year-long time steps, which does not allow for a precise estimation of the timing of farmer response after disease outbreaks.
source: One limitation of these two studies is that the dynamics were observed over year-long time steps, which does not allow for a precise estimation of the timing of farmer response after the occurrence of disease outbreaks and the potential feedback effect of this response onto the resulting outbreaks or epidemics.
evidence: This is an inference based on the cited studies' methodologies.

claim: HPAI has been endemic in Vietnam since its initial emergence in 2003–2004.
source: The disease has been endemic in the country since its initial emergence in 2003–2004 (Delabouglise et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to published literature.

claim: Small-scale poultry farming is practiced by more than seven million Vietnamese households.
source: Small-scale poultry farming is practiced by more than seven million Vietnamese households, mostly on a scale of fewer than 100 birds per farm (General Statistics Office of Vietnam, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to official statistics.

claim: Most Vietnamese small-scale poultry farms have fewer than 100 birds per farm.
source: Small-scale poultry farming is practiced by more than seven million Vietnamese households, mostly on a scale of fewer than 100 birds per farm (General Statistics Office of Vietnam, 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to official statistics.

claim: Newcastle disease, fowl cholera, and Gumboro are endemic in Vietnam's poultry sector despite the availability of vaccines for their control.
source: In addition to HPAI, other infectious diseases severely affect this economic sector, including Newcastle disease, fowl cholera, and Gumboro, which are all endemic despite the availability of vaccines for their control (OIE, 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to OIE documentation.

claim: Fifty three farms were monitored from June 2015 to January 2017.
source: Fifty three farms were monitored from June 2015 to January 2017.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study design and data collection.

claim: Monthly questionnaires were used to collect farm-level information on poultry demographics, mortality, and management by farmers.
source: Monthly questionnaires were used to collect farm-level information on poultry demographics (number, introduction, death and departure of birds), mortality (cause of death, observed clinical symptoms) and management by farmers.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methodology.

claim: The main poultry species kept on these farms was chicken, with ducks and Muscovy ducks as the other two primary relevant species held.
source: The main poultry species kept on these farms was chicken, with ducks and Muscovy ducks as the other two primary relevant species held.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study observations.

claim: Farmers kept an average number of 79 chickens, 53 ducks and 7 Muscovy ducks per farm over the 20 month study period.
source: Farmers kept an average number of 79 chickens, 53 ducks and 7 Muscovy ducks per farm over the 20 month study period.
evidence: This is a direct statement of descriptive statistics from the study data.

source: Each farm's poultry were classified into 'flocks', defined as groups of birds of the same age, species, and production type.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the study methodology.

source: Broiler chicken flocks were kept for 15.5 weeks on average after which most chickens were harvested and a minority was consumed or kept on the farm for breeding and egg production (Delabouglise et al., 2019).

source: A total of 1656 broiler chicken flock-months were available for analysis.

source: They belonged to 391 chicken flocks present on 48 farms.

source: In 18.8% of flock-months non-sudden outbreaks (ONS) were observed in chickens on the same farm, 1.6% of flock-months saw sudden outbreaks (OS) in chickens on the same farm, and 7.2% of flock-months saw disease outbreaks in poultry of other species on the same farm (Table 1).

claim: In 1.6% of flock-months sudden outbreaks (OS) were observed in chickens on the same farm.
source: In 18.8% of flock-months non-sudden outbreaks (ONS) were observed in chickens on the same farm, 1.6% of flock-months saw sudden outbreaks (OS) in chickens on the same farm, and 7.2% of flock-months saw disease outbreaks in poultry of other species on the same farm (Table 1).

source: In 18.8% of flock-months non-sudden outbreaks (ONS) were observed in chickens on the same farm, 1.6% of flock-months saw sudden outbreaks (OS) in chickens on the same farm, and 7.2% of flock-months saw disease outbreaks in poultry of other species on the same farm (Table 1).

claim: Out of 1656 broiler chicken flock months, 1503 flock-months were selected for the harvest analysis after excluding data points with new-born chicks and flock-months in which all the chickens had died.
source: Out of 1656 broiler chicken flock months, 1503 flock-months were selected for the harvest analysis after excluding data points with new-born chicks and flock-months in which all the chickens had died (see Materials and methods).

source: No harvest occurred in 995 flock-months, complete harvest occurred in 258 flock-months, and partial harvest occurred in 250 flock-months.

source: No harvest occurred in 995 flock-months, complete harvest occurred in 258 flock-months, and partial harvest occurred in 250 flock-months.

source: No harvest occurred in 995 flock-months, complete harvest occurred in 258 flock-months, and partial harvest occurred in 250 flock-months.

source: The probability of harvest during a month, with partial harvests weighted appropriately, was 23.9%.

source: Excluding flock-months of already vaccinated chickens (and some with missing data), 1318 flock-months were selected for the AI vaccination analysis (see Materials and methods).

source: AI vaccination was performed in 7.5% (99/1318) of flock-months.

source: The 99 vaccinated flocks were from 29 different farms (out of 48 farms keeping broiler chickens).

source: For the disinfection model, 858 farm-months belonging to 52 farms were included (see Materials and methods).

source: During 552 farm-months the farm was fully disinfected, during 259 farm-months the farm was not disinfected at all, and during 47 farm-months disinfection was performed for some (but not all) of the flocks present in the farm.

claim: During 259 farm-months the farm was not disinfected at all.
source: During 552 farm-months the farm was fully disinfected, during 259 farm-months the farm was not disinfected at all, and during 47 farm-months disinfection was performed for some (but not all) of the flocks present in the farm.

claim: During 47 farm-months disinfection was performed for some (but not all) of the flocks present in the farm.
source: During 552 farm-months the farm was fully disinfected, during 259 farm-months the farm was not disinfected at all, and during 47 farm-months disinfection was performed for some (but not all) of the flocks present in the farm.

claim: The probability of disinfection during a month, with partial disinfections weighted appropriately, was 67.4%.
source: The probability of disinfection during a month, with partial disinfections weighted appropriately, was 67.4%.

claim: There was no statistical support for a temporal auto-correlation of the probability of harvest of broiler chicken flocks on a given farm.
source: There was no statistical support for a temporal auto-correlation of the probability of harvest of broiler chicken flocks on a given farm (Table 2).

claim: A threshold value of 16 birds per flock gave the lowest Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) when using a categorical variable indicating small flock or large flock.
source: A threshold value of 16 birds per flock gave the lowest Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) (when using a categorical variable indicating small flock or large flock), and flocks of 16 birds or fewer (52% of all flocks) were designated as small while flocks of 17 or more (48% of all flocks) were designated as large.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: Flocks of 16 birds or fewer represented 52% of all flocks.
source: A threshold value of 16 birds per flock gave the lowest Akaike Information Criterion (AIC) (when using a categorical variable indicating small flock or large flock), and flocks of 16 birds or fewer (52% of all flocks) were designated as small while flocks of 17 or more (48% of all flocks) were designated as large.
evidence: This is a direct statement of descriptive statistics from the study data.

claim: Flocks of 17 or more birds represented 48% of all flocks.

evidence: This is a direct statement of descriptive statistics from the study data.

claim: The probability of harvest was found to be strongly dependent on the difference (δt) between the flock age and the anticipated age at maturity, with older flocks being more likely to be sold.
source: As expected, the probability of harvest was found to be strongly dependent on the difference (δt) between the flock age and the anticipated age at maturity, with older flocks being more likely to be sold.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: The probability of harvest was close to zero when δt < −15 weeks.
source: The probability of harvest was close to zero when δt < −15 weeks, i.e. flocks that are more than 15 weeks away from maturity.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: The probability of harvest increased steeply from δt = −10 to δt = 0.
source: The probability of harvest increased steeply from δt = −10 to δt = 0.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: For δt > 0 (flocks past their age at maturity), the probability of harvest was consistently high but lower than 100% and did not depend on age.
source: For δt > 0 (flocks past their age at maturity), the probability of harvest was consistently high but lower than 100% and did not depend on age.
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: Larger flocks had a steeper increase in harvest probability as a function of δt.
source: Larger flocks had a steeper increase in harvest probability as a function of δt; once past the age at maturity (δt > 0), the estimated probability of harvest for large flocks was higher (interquartile range: 41–61%) than for small flocks (interquartile range: 30–41%) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 2.

claim: Once past the age at maturity (δt > 0), the estimated probability of harvest for large flocks was higher (interquartile range: 41–61%) than for small flocks (interquartile range: 30–41%).
source: Larger flocks had a steeper increase in harvest probability as a function of δt; once past the age at maturity (δt > 0), the estimated probability of harvest for large flocks was higher (interquartile range: 41–61%) than for small flocks (interquartile range: 30–41%) (Figure 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 2.

claim: The probability of harvest of small flocks was significantly higher on farms that had experienced a non-sudden outbreak (ONS) in chickens in the same month (odds ratio (OR) = 2.06; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.23–3.45).
source: The probability of harvest of small flocks was significantly higher on farms that had experienced a non-sudden outbreak (ONS) in chickens in the same month (odds ratio (OR) = 2.06; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.23–3.45) or the previous month (OR = 2.06; 95% CI: 1.17–3.62) and was lower on farms that had experienced an ONS in chickens two months prior (OR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.19–0.92).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: The probability of harvest of small flocks was significantly higher on farms that had experienced a non-sudden outbreak (ONS) in chickens in the previous month (OR = 2.06; 95% CI: 1.17–3.62).
source: The probability of harvest of small flocks was significantly higher on farms that had experienced a non-sudden outbreak (ONS) in chickens in the same month (odds ratio (OR) = 2.06; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.23–3.45) or the previous month (OR = 2.06; 95% CI: 1.17–3.62) and was lower on farms that had experienced an ONS in chickens two months prior (OR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.19–0.92).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: The probability of harvest of small flocks was lower on farms that had experienced an ONS in chickens two months prior (OR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.19–0.92).
source: The probability of harvest of small flocks was significantly higher on farms that had experienced a non-sudden outbreak (ONS) in chickens in the same month (odds ratio (OR) = 2.06; 95% confidence interval (CI): 1.23–3.45) or the previous month (OR = 2.06; 95% CI: 1.17–3.62) and was lower on farms that had experienced an ONS in chickens two months prior (OR = 0.41; 95% CI: 0.19–0.92).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: The probability of harvest of small flocks was much higher on farms that had experienced a sudden outbreak (OS) in the same month (OR = 9.34: 95% CI: 2.13–40.94).
source: The probability of harvest of small flocks was much higher on farms that had experienced a sudden outbreak (OS) in the same month (OR = 9.34: 95% CI: 2.13–40.94).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results.

claim: Estimated mean harvest proportions of small flocks were 17% (no outbreak), 28% (ONS), and 56% (OS) when considering outbreaks occurring in the same month.
source: Estimated mean harvest proportions of small flocks were 17% (no outbreak), 28% (ONS), and 56% (OS) when considering outbreaks occurring in the same month; this corresponded to harvest increases of 56% and 214% for ONS and OS outbreaks, respectively.
evidence: This is a direct statement of model predictions based on the statistical analysis.

claim: Harvest increases of 56% and 214% were observed for ONS and OS outbreaks, respectively, when considering outbreaks occurring in the same month.

evidence: This is a direct statement of model predictions based on the statistical analysis.

claim: Estimated mean harvest proportion was 18% (no outbreak) and 28% (ONS) when considering outbreaks one month prior.
source: Estimated mean harvest proportion was 18% (no outbreak) and 28% (ONS) when considering outbreaks one month prior; this corresponded to a 56% increase in harvest in case of ONS one month prior.

claim: A 56% increase in harvest was observed in case of ONS one month prior.
source: Estimated mean harvest proportion was 18% (no outbreak) and 28% (ONS) when considering outbreaks one month prior; this corresponded to a 56% increase in harvest in case of ONS one month prior.
evidence: This is a direct statement of model predictions based on the statistical analysis.

claim: Mean harvest proportions were 20% (no outbreak) and 11% (ONS) when considering outbreaks two months prior, indicating a 47% decrease in harvest in case of ONS two months prior.
source: Mean harvest proportions were 20% (no outbreak) and 11% (ONS) when considering outbreaks two months prior, indicating a 47% decrease in harvest in case of ONS two months prior.

claim: Probability of vaccination was almost zero for flocks of 16 birds or fewer.
source: The likelihood of broiler chicken vaccination against AI strongly increased with flock size; probability of vaccination was almost zero for flocks of 16 birds or fewer and nearly 100% for flocks of more than 200 birds (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Probability of vaccination was nearly 100% for flocks of more than 200 birds.
source: The likelihood of broiler chicken vaccination against AI strongly increased with flock size; probability of vaccination was almost zero for flocks of 16 birds or fewer and nearly 100% for flocks of more than 200 birds (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is a direct statement of statistical analysis results with reference to Figure 3A.

claim: Vaccination was preferentially performed at 4.3 weeks of age.
source: Vaccination was preferentially performed at 4.3 weeks of age (Figure 3B).

claim: The number of broiler Muscovy ducks present in the farm had a negative effect (p=0.03) on the probability of AI vaccination.

claim: The number of layer ducks and layer Muscovy ducks had a positive effect (both p=0.03) on the probability of AI vaccination.

claim: Temporal auto-correlation was not observed for the harvest or vaccination models (both p>0.3).
